Genesis.author: The book never names its author [[eob:Genesis]]. Until the 1600s Jews and Christians almost unanimously named Moses, and many still hold that view [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]] [[bo:18623]]. Many modern scholars see it as woven from older traditions, given its final shape by a priestly editor during or after the exile in Babylon [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]].
Genesis.date: If Moses wrote it, in the wilderness after the Exodus: about 1445 BC on the early dating [[bo:18623]], or by 1240 BC at the latest on the later one [[eob:Genesis]]. Scholars who see several sources place its final form during or after the exile [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]].
Genesis.to: The people of Israel, to help them understand their roots in Abraham, Isaac and Jacob [[bo:18623]], and as the groundwork for the rest of the books of Moses [[eob:Genesis]].
Genesis.why: The book never states its purpose [[eob:Genesis]]. It is a selective history that lays the foundation for the whole Bible [[bo:18623]]: creation, the spread of sin, and God’s promise to bless all nations through Abraham’s family [[bible:Genesis 12:1-3]].
Genesis.story: Chapters 1–11 tell the early history of humankind, and chapters 12–50 the story of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph [[eob:Genesis]]. God’s call of Abram begins a new history of blessing [[nabre:genesis/12]], and Paul says the promised offspring is Christ [[bible:Galatians 3:16]].
Genesis.genre: Narrative history, organised under ten headings, “these are the generations of…” (Hebrew toledot, best translated “history”) [[eob:Genesis]] [[bo:18623]].
Genesis.debate: How Genesis was written: the theory of J, E, D and P sources, and its critics [[eob:Genesis]] [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]]; and how its creation and flood accounts compare with other ancient Near Eastern stories, such as the Gilgamesh and Atrahasis epics [[nabre:genesis/6]] [[eob:Genesis]].
Genesis.structureNote: The book falls into two halves, the early history (1–11) and the story of the patriarchs (12–50) [[eob:Genesis]]; the outline below follows the main characters of the text.

Exodus.author: The book does not name its author [[eob:Book-Exodus]]. Very early Jewish tradition held that Moses wrote all of it, and many still hold that view [[eob:Book-Exodus]] [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]]. Many modern scholars see it as woven from older traditions; the worship chapters (25–31, 35–40) belong to the Priestly material [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]].
Exodus.date: The events: about 1446 BC on the early dating, or about 1260 BC on the late dating, which links the city of Raamses (1:11) with Pharaoh Rameses II; both are held by evangelical scholars [[ref:esv-exodus-date]]. The evidence is not enough for a final decision, but points to the second half of the second millennium BC [[eob:Book-Exodus]].
Exodus.to: The people of Israel, as the story of how God made them his own nation [[nabre:exodus/0]].
Exodus.why: It tells how God freed Israel from Egypt, bound them to himself in the covenant at Sinai, and came to dwell among them [[nabre:exodus/0]]. Its great themes are redemption, covenant, law and worship [[eob:Book-Exodus]].
Exodus.story: The name Exodus is Greek for “departure”; in Hebrew the book is called Shemoth, “Names”, from its opening words [[nabre:exodus/0]]. The rescue from Egypt is remembered every year at Passover [[bible:Exodus 12:14]], and the New Testament calls Christ “our Passover” [[bible:1 Corinthians 5:7]].
Exodus.genre: About half narrative, the first nineteen chapters, and about half law and instructions for worship [[eob:Book-Exodus]].
Exodus.debate: The date of the Exodus [[ref:esv-exodus-date]]; why no Egyptian king is named and why Egyptian monuments are silent, which is expected since defeats were not recorded [[eob:Book-Exodus]]; how its laws compare with Hammurabi’s code, with which direct parallels are fairly few [[eob:Book-Exodus]]; and how the book was composed from sources [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]].
Exodus.structureNote: The NABRE divides the book into eight parts [[nabre:exodus/0]]; the outline below follows them.

Leviticus.author: The book does not name its author [[eob:Leviticus]]. It presents its laws as given by God through Moses [[bible:Leviticus 26:46]], and some scholars defend that view [[eob:Leviticus]]. Many see it as part of the Priestly tradition (P), with signs of development within it [[nabre:leviticus/0]] [[eob:Leviticus]].
Leviticus.date: On the traditional view, the time at Sinai [[eob:Leviticus]]. Critical scholars date the Priestly material later, in its final form no later than about 550 BC on one view, or in the 400s BC on another [[eob:Leviticus]].
Leviticus.to: The people of Israel and their priests. Its laws are meant to shape the whole way of life of those who hear them [[nabre:leviticus/0]].
Leviticus.why: It sets out how the holy God can live among an unholy people [[eob:Leviticus]]: sacrifices, purity and holiness, the priesthood, the sanctuary and the feasts [[nabre:leviticus/0]].
Leviticus.story: It carries on the story of Exodus and stands at the centre of the five books of Moses [[nabre:leviticus/0]]. Its Hebrew name is its first word, “And he called” [[eob:Leviticus]]. Hebrews reads its priests and sacrifices as a shadow of Christ’s work [[eob:Leviticus]] [[bible:Hebrews 10:1]].
Leviticus.genre: Laws for worship and daily life, with a few short narratives [[nabre:leviticus/0]].
Leviticus.debate: How and when the book was composed from sources [[eob:Leviticus]]; what the verb kipper, “atone”, means: to wipe away, to cover, or to pay a ransom [[eob:Leviticus]]; and whether the Holiness laws came before or after Ezekiel, which cannot be shown with certainty [[eob:Leviticus]].
Leviticus.structureNote: The outline follows the five parts of the NABRE introduction [[nabre:leviticus/0]].

Numbers.author: Like the other books of the Pentateuch, it has traditionally been credited to Moses [[easton:Numbers-Book]]; it says Moses wrote down the list of Israel’s journeys [[bible:Numbers 33:2]]. Many modern scholars see it, like the rest of the Pentateuch, as woven from several traditions [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]].
Numbers.date: The events cover about thirty-eight years, from the second year after the Exodus to the fortieth [[easton:Numbers-Book]] [[nabre:numbers/0]]. Scholars who see several sources place the Pentateuch’s final form during or after the exile [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]].
Numbers.to: The people of Israel, who were about to enter the land God had promised [[nabre:numbers/0]].
Numbers.why: It follows two generations: the one that refused to trust God and died in the wilderness, and the new one being prepared to enter the land [[nabre:numbers/0]]. Its laws are set within the story [[nabre:numbers/0]].
Numbers.story: It continues the journey begun in Exodus [[nabre:numbers/0]]. The New Testament recalls its bronze serpent, Korah’s rebellion, Balaam’s prophecies and the water from the rock [[nabre:numbers/0]] [[bible:John 3:14-15]] [[bible:1 Corinthians 10:4]], and Hebrews uses the wilderness generation as a warning against unbelief [[bible:Hebrews 3:17-19]].
Numbers.genre: Law and history together, with two censuses, travel lists and the poetic oracles of Balaam [[nabre:numbers/0]].
structure: Rebellion and forty years in the wilderness
A new generation prepares to enter the land
Numbers.debate: How the book was composed [[nabre:thepentateuch/0]]; the route through the wilderness, since the list of stages is not complete and many places are not known [[nabre:numbers/33]]; and what exactly Moses’s sin at Meribah was, which the text does not make clear [[nabre:numbers/20]].
Numbers.structureNote: The NABRE divides the book into three parts [[nabre:numbers/0]]; the outline below follows them.

Deuteronomy.author: It is presented as three speeches of Moses [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]]. Those who hold that Moses wrote it point to its likeness to Hittite treaties of the second millennium BC [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]]; an editor completed it after his death [[bo:885]]. Others hold that it was written by an unknown author in the 600s BC, in King Josiah’s time [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]].
Deuteronomy.date: If by Moses, the 1300s or 1200s BC [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]], or about 1406 BC on the early dating of the Exodus [[bo:885]]. The NABRE judges it was probably composed over three centuries, from the 700s BC to after the exile [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]].
Deuteronomy.to: The new generation of Israel on the plains of Moab, about to enter the promised land [[nabre:deuteronomy/1]] [[tosn:Deuteronomy 4:13]].
Deuteronomy.why: To call Israel to choose between loving the LORD and keeping his commands, which brings blessing, or serving other gods, which brings curse [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]]: so that the nation might live and possess the land [[bo:885]].
Deuteronomy.story: Its language and ideas shape the books from Joshua to Kings [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]]. More than 80 Old Testament quotations in the New Testament come from it, and Jesus quoted it when tempted and when naming the greatest commandment [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]].
Deuteronomy.genre: Speeches of Moses that follow the pattern of an ancient covenant treaty, with laws, blessings and curses [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]] [[tosn:Deuteronomy 1:1]].
structure: Third address: covenant renewal and farewell
Deuteronomy.debate: Whether Moses wrote it or it was written in Josiah’s time [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]]; its relation to the book of the law found in the temple in 622 BC [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]]; and how closely it follows Hittite treaty forms [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]]. Its Greek name, “second law”, can mislead, since it is not a simple repeat of the law [[tbd:004:Deuteronomy, Book of]].
Deuteronomy.structureNote: The NABRE divides the book into three addresses of Moses and the account of his death [[nabre:deuteronomy/0]]; the outline below follows them.

Joshua.author: The book does not say. The Talmud names Joshua, perhaps because he “wrote these words” of the covenant renewal (24:26) [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]] [[bible:Joshua 24:26]]. The NABRE treats it as part of the Deuteronomistic History, written for Israel late in the time of the kings [[nabre:joshua/0]].
Joshua.date: There are no clear markers, and scholars do not agree [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]]. A conservative view dates the writing between 1375 and 1045 BC; critical scholars suggest the 600s BC or the exile [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]].
Joshua.to: Israel, to show how the LORD gave them the land and how they might prosper in it [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]], and to warn them against losing it [[nabre:joshua/0]].
Joshua.why: To show Joshua following in Moses’s footsteps, the LORD giving the land, and the conditions for keeping it: trusting the LORD and staying united and faithful [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]] [[nabre:joshua/0]].
Joshua.story: God’s promise of the land is kept: “Nothing failed of any good thing which Yahweh had spoken” [[bible:Joshua 21:45]]. Joshua’s name means “the LORD saves”, the same name as Jesus [[nabre:numbers/13]].
Joshua.genre: History, the first of the books the Hebrew Bible calls the Former Prophets [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]], with lists of tribal lands that preserve older traditions [[nabre:joshua/0]].
Joshua.debate: When and by whom it was written [[tbd:010:Joshua, Book of]]; how its swift conquest fits Judges 1, which suggests a slow and piecemeal settlement [[nabre:joshua/0]]; and how to read the total destruction it describes, which the NABRE calls an idealisation, set against the New Testament command to love enemies [[nabre:joshua/0]].
Joshua.structureNote: The NABRE divides the book into three parts [[nabre:joshua/0]]; the outline below follows them, with the conquest in two halves.

Judges.author: Unknown. It was almost certainly not Samuel, as later tradition suggested; a later writer probably compiled it from older written sources [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.date: The final editing reflects the early days of Israel’s kings [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]]. The period itself began about 1370–1360 BC on the early dating of the Exodus, or near the end of the 1200s BC on the later one [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.to: Israel under its first kings, explaining why the tribes did not take all the land and pointing toward a king who would shepherd the people [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.why: It shows an age that repeated itself without progress, defends God’s justice and patience when Israel kept disobeying, and supports the idea of a shepherd king [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.story: A new generation falls into a cycle of rebellion and partial rescue [[tosn:Judges 2:10-19]]. It ends: “In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did that which was right in his own eyes” [[bible:Judges 21:25]], looking toward God’s covenant with David [[tosn:Judges 21:25]].
Judges.genre: Hero stories of twelve judges from different regions, framed by an introduction and two closing stories [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]] [[tosn:Judges 17:1-21:25]].
structure: Everyone did what was right in his own eyes
Judges.debate: How long the period of the judges lasted, which depends on the date of the Exodus [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]]; and whether the book argues for David’s rule rather than Saul’s, as some scholars think [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].
Judges.structureNote: The outline follows the book’s introduction, the stories of the judges and its two closing stories [[tbd:010:Judges, Book of]].

Ruth.author: Unknown [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]]. Since it closes with David’s family line, it was probably written after David began to reign, perhaps by someone close to him such as Samuel, Nathan or Abiathar [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].
Ruth.date: The events took place around 1100 BC, in the days of the judges [[tosn:Ruth 1:1]]. It was likely written after David became king [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].
Ruth.to: Israel, perhaps to show that David’s family was the chosen royal line, and to explain how a faithful Moabite woman became part of Israel [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].
Ruth.why: It shows God’s kindness reaching even those not born Israelites, and Ruth’s love for Naomi as a model of devotion [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].
Ruth.story: Ruth becomes King David’s great-grandmother [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]] [[bible:Ruth 4:17]], and she appears in Jesus’s family tree [[bible:Matthew 1:5]].
Ruth.genre: A short story that ends with a family line of ten generations, from Perez to David [[tosn:Ruth 4:18-22]].
Ruth.debate: When it was written, which affects what its purpose was [[tbd:018:Ruth, Book of]].

1 Samuel.author: Unknown. It cannot have been Samuel alone, since his death is reported in 25:1 [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]. Some suggest Samuel with the prophets Nathan and Gad (1 Chronicles 29:29), but the real author cannot be determined [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.date: Its final form comes some time after Solomon’s death and the division of the kingdom in 930 BC [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.to: Israel, about what kind of king fits God’s covenant [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.why: Israel moves from judges to kings. Kingship as the people demanded it denied the covenant, Saul’s reign failed it, and David’s, though imperfect, truly reflected it [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.story: Hannah’s song looks ahead to kingship in Israel and ultimately to Christ [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]. God looks at the heart, not appearances [[bible:1 Samuel 16:7]].
1 Samuel.genre: Historical narrative with poetry, such as Hannah’s song (2:1–10) [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]. 1 and 2 Samuel were one book until the Greek translators split them in two [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
1 Samuel.debate: Who wrote it, and how its mixed feelings about kingship fit together; the book resolves them in chapter 12 [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].

2 Samuel.author: Unknown. 1 and 2 Samuel were originally one book, and its real author cannot be determined [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
2 Samuel.date: David ruled the strongest kingdom of the region about 1000 BC [[tbd:004:David]]. The book reached its final form some time after the kingdom split in 930 BC [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
2 Samuel.to: Israel, about David’s reign and what kind of king fits God’s covenant [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].
2 Samuel.why: David becomes king of all Israel, makes Jerusalem its centre, and receives God’s promise of a lasting dynasty [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]; then his sin with Bathsheba brings trouble on his family [[bsn:2 Samuel 11:1–14:33]].
2 Samuel.story: God promises David a house that will last forever [[bible:2 Samuel 7:16]], a promise fulfilled in the eternal reign of Jesus Christ [[tosn:2 Samuel 7:19]].
2 Samuel.genre: Historical narrative with poetry, such as David’s laments and his song in chapter 22 [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]]. Chapters 21–24 are arranged by topic, not by time [[tosn:2 Samuel 21:1–24:25]].
2 Samuel.debate: Who wrote it and when it took its final form [[tbd:019:Samuel, Books of First and Second]].

1 Kings.author: Unknown; the book is anonymous [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. Jewish tradition in the Talmud names Jeremiah, and an origin among the prophets fits the evidence well [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. It draws on official royal annals, “the chronicles of the kings” [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.date: The events run from Solomon’s accession to the divided kingdoms [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]; Solomon’s fourth year was about 967 BC [[tosn:1 Kings 6:1]] and the kingdom split under Rehoboam in 931 BC [[tosn:1 Kings 12:1]]. 1 and 2 Kings were completed in exile, likely between 561 and 539 BC [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.to: The exiles, who were asking how and why Jerusalem and the temple could fall [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.why: Solomon’s glory and temple, the split into Israel and Judah, and Elijah’s stand against Baal. The writer weighs this history by the standard of Deuteronomy [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.story: Each king is judged by faithfulness to God, not by political success [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]], and the book keeps showing words spoken by the prophets coming true [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.genre: History written for theological reasons, not a modern history textbook [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
1 Kings.debate: Who compiled it, and how the dates given for the kings of Israel and Judah fit together into one timeline [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].

2 Kings.author: Unknown; 1 and 2 Kings are anonymous [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. Jewish tradition names Jeremiah, and an origin among the prophets fits the evidence well [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.date: It covers the divided kingdoms, the fall of Samaria in 722 BC [[tosn:2 Kings 17:5–6]], Jerusalem’s fall in 586 BC, and Jehoiachin’s release about 561 BC [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]]. Written in exile, likely between 561 and 539 BC [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.to: The exiles, asking how and why the temple and David’s throne had fallen [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.why: Elisha’s miracles, the fall of Israel to Assyria and of Judah to Babylon, with a few faithful kings along the way. The writer measures the history by Deuteronomy [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.story: The exile is explained as the result of turning from God [[bible:2 Kings 17:7]]. It ends with Jehoiachin released, a hint that God would bring his people home [[tosn:2 Kings 25:27–30]].
2 Kings.genre: History written for theological reasons, drawing on royal annals [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].
2 Kings.debate: How the reigns of the kings fit into one timeline, and how the book compares with Assyrian and Babylonian records [[tosn:2 Kings 17:5–6]] [[tbd:011:Kings, Books of First and Second]].

1 Chronicles.author: Unknown, usually called “the Chronicler” [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]]. The Talmud says Ezra wrote it, and many scholars agree, but there is no general agreement [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.date: Probably around 400 BC, in the Persian period [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.to: Jews living in Jerusalem under Persian rule after the exile [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.why: With David’s kingdom gone politically, the Chronicler finds the key to history in God’s covenant with David, and gives temple worship great weight [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.story: It retells Israel’s story from Adam to David. Chronicles tells of times David was faithful and leaves some of his failures to 2 Samuel [[bsn:1 Chronicles 9:35–20:8]].
1 Chronicles.genre: Genealogies (chapters 1–9) and the reign of David (chapters 10–29) [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
1 Chronicles.debate: Who wrote it and when, and whether the same author wrote Ezra and Nehemiah [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].

2 Chronicles.author: Unknown, usually called “the Chronicler”; the Talmud names Ezra, but there is no general agreement [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.date: Probably around 400 BC, in the Persian period [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.to: Jews in Jerusalem under Persian rule, for whom temple worship mattered greatly [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.why: Solomon’s reign, the kings of Judah, and an epilogue on the exile and return [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.story: It ends with Cyrus inviting God’s people to go up to Jerusalem [[bible:2 Chronicles 36:23]]. Chronicles stands at the very end of the Hebrew Bible [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.genre: History drawing on earlier records, retelling Samuel and Kings with its own concerns [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].
2 Chronicles.debate: Who wrote it and when, and whether its author also wrote Ezra and Nehemiah [[tbd:003:Chronicles, Books of First and Second]].

Ezra.author: Many believe Ezra himself collected and wrote the material; parts are told in his own words [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]].
Ezra.date: The events run from Cyrus’s decree after he took Babylon in 539 BC to Ezra’s work under Artaxerxes I (465–424 BC) [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]]. Ezra came about 13 years before Nehemiah, who arrived in 445 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]].
Ezra.to: The Jews who returned from exile under Persian rule [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]].
Ezra.why: Exiles return from Babylon, rebuild the temple [[bible:Ezra 6:15]], and Ezra the scribe teaches God’s law [[bible:Ezra 7:10]].
Ezra.story: God moved a king who did not know him, Cyrus of Persia, to let his people go home [[tosn:Ezra 1:1]].
Ezra.genre: History with official letters written in Aramaic and a first-person account by Ezra [[tbd:002:Book of Ezra]].
structure: The first return and the temple
Ezra.debate: Whether Ezra came before Nehemiah [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]], and how to understand the divorces of chapter 10, for which the law gave no clear instructions [[tosn:Ezra 10:4]].

Nehemiah.author: Nehemiah tells much of it in his own words [[bible:Nehemiah 1:1]]. Ezra and Nehemiah formed one book in the early Hebrew Bible [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].
Nehemiah.date: Nehemiah came to Jerusalem in 445 BC, under Artaxerxes I [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].
Nehemiah.to: The Jews who had returned to Judah under Persian rule [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].
Nehemiah.why: Nehemiah, the Persian king’s cupbearer, rebuilds Jerusalem’s walls and leads the people to renew their covenant with God [[bible:Nehemiah 1:11]] [[bible:Nehemiah 10:29]].
Nehemiah.story: One of the last of the Jewish historical books [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].
Nehemiah.genre: First-person memoir with lists and a covenant ceremony [[bible:Nehemiah 7:5]] [[bible:Nehemiah 9:38]].
Nehemiah.debate: The exact order of Ezra’s and Nehemiah’s work; the book’s message is clear either way [[tbd:002:Book of Nehemiah]].

Esther.author: Unknown. Esther 9:20 says Mordecai “wrote these things”, which may mean he wrote part or all of it [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]].
Esther.date: Set under Xerxes, who died in 465 BC [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]]. When it was written is uncertain: some say shortly after 465 BC, others much later [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]].
Esther.to: Jews living in the Persian empire, and to explain the feast of Purim [[bible:Esther 9:26-28]].
Esther.why: A Jewish queen of Persia risks her life to save her people from a plot to destroy them [[bible:Esther 4:16]].
Esther.story: God’s name never appears, perhaps because the book was meant for the official Persian court record [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]]; yet the reversals show God’s guiding hand [[tosn:Esther 7:9]].
Esther.genre: A court story written by someone who knew Persian court life well [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]].
Esther.debate: When and why it was written, and the extra passages in the Greek version [[tbd:002:Book of Esther]] [[tbd:005:Esther, Additions to]].

Psalms.author: Many writers. The Hebrew titles credit David with 73 psalms, Asaph with 12 and the sons of Korah with 11, Solomon with two, and Moses and Ethan with one each [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]]. The titles were added early and are a reasonably reliable guide [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.date: From David’s time, around 1000 BC [[tbd:004:David]], to after the exile [[tosn:Psalm 126:1–6]]. The collection was complete before the Greek translation at the end of the 200s BC [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.to: God’s people at worship, in every situation of life [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.why: Every emotion, from bitter complaint to joyful praise, brought into communion with God [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.story: The apostles use the Psalms to describe the life and work of Jesus the Messiah [[tosn:Psalm 1:1–6]]; most royal psalms are also messianic [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.genre: Poetry in five books (1–41, 42–72, 73–89, 90–106, 107–150), perhaps echoing the five books of Moses, each of the first four ending with a doxology [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
Psalms.debate: What the titles mean: “of David” usually means by David, but with groups it may mean from their collection [[tbd:016:Psalms, Book of]].
